In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the morning brightness, and by the night when it is still, your Lord has neither forsaken you nor come to hate you.﴾

God Most High says: ﴿By the morning brightness. And by the night when it is still.﴾ The discussion of *ad-duha* (the morning brightness) has already been given above [[See p. 72 and what follows in this part.]]. Here it means the daytime, since the verse pairs it with ﴿the night﴾, so the day is set against the night. In the surah of al-A'raf, God says: ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them by night while they sleep? Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them in the morning brightness while they play?﴾ [al-A'raf 7:97–98], meaning by day. Qatadah, Muqatil and Ja'far al-Sadiq said: He swore by the morning brightness in which Allah spoke to Musa, and by the night of the Mi'raj (the Night Journey and Ascension). It has also been said that it is the hour in which the magicians fell down prostrate. The proof of this is God's words: ﴿and that the people be gathered in the morning brightness﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:59].

The scholars of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said concerning this and similar verses: there is an omission (*idmar*) in it, and its sense is "by the Lord of the morning brightness."

*"Why is it our fault that the sea of your uncle's sons surged,*
*while your sea is still and does not hide the small water-beetles?"* [[In the Diwan of al-A'sha: "Atwa'iduni an jasha..." The *da'amis* is the plural of *da'mus*, a small creature found in stagnant water.]]

The reciter (*ar-rajiz*) said:

*"Oh, how I love the white moon and the still night,*
*and a road like the weaver's cloth."*

Jarir said:

*"We certainly shot you with glances on the day they departed,*
*looking through the gaps of the curtains, with still eyes."*

Al-Dahhak said: *saja* means it covered everything. Al-Asma'i said: *sajw al-layl* is its covering of the day, just as a man is covered with a garment. Al-Hasan said: it was overcast with its darkness, and Ibn Abbas said the same. Also from him: when it departs. Also from him: when it grows dark. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: when it approached. This is also reported from Qatadah. Ibn Abi Najih reported from Mujahid: *saja* means it became level. The first view is the best known in the language: *saja* means became still, that is, people became still in it, just as one says "a fasting day" and "a standing night." It has also been said that its stillness is the settling and levelling of its darkness.

It is said: *"wa'd-duha, wa'l-layli idha saja"* means: His worshippers who worship Him at the time of the morning brightness, and His worshippers who worship Him at night when it grows dark. It is also said: *ad-duha* means the light of Paradise when it is illuminated, and *al-layl idha saja* means the darkness of the night when it grows dark. It is also said: *ad-duha* means the light that is in the hearts of the knowers (*al-arifin*), like the state of day, and *al-layl idha saja* means the blackness that is in the hearts of the disbelievers, like the state of night. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, swore by these things.

﴿Your Lord has neither forsaken you nor come to hate you.﴾ This is the answer to the oath. Jibril (peace be upon him) had been slow in coming to the Prophet (ﷺ), so the polytheists said: "Muhammad's Lord has forsaken him and hated him." So the verse was revealed. Ibn Jurayj said: revelation was withheld from him for twelve days. Ibn Abbas said: fifteen days. It has also been said: twenty-five days. Muqatil said: forty days. The polytheists said: "Muhammad's Lord has forsaken him and hated him. If his matter came from Allah, He would have followed it up, as He used to do with the prophets before him."

In al-Bukhari, from Jundab ibn Sufyan, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became ill and did not get up for a night or two nights (or three), then a woman [[She was al-Awra' bint Harb, sister of Abu Sufyan, the firewood carrier, wife of Abu Lahab.]] came and said: "O Muhammad, I hope that your devil has left you. I have not seen him come near you for two nights or three." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿By the morning brightness, and by the night when it is still. Your Lord has neither forsaken you nor come to hate you.﴾

In al-Tirmidhi, from Jundab al-Bajali, who said: I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) in a cave, and his finger bled. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: [*Are you anything but a bleeding finger? And in the way of Allah you have suffered what you have suffered.*] He said: Jibril was slow to come to him, and the polytheists said: "Muhammad has been forsaken." So Allah, Blessed and Exalted, revealed: ﴿Your Lord has neither forsaken you nor come to hate you.﴾ This is a hadith that is *hasan sahih* (good and sound). Al-Tirmidhi did not mention: "so he did not get up for a night or two nights or three"; al-Tirmidhi omitted it. Al-Bukhari mentioned it, and it is the most authentic of what has been said about this. And Allah knows best.

Al-Tha'labi also mentioned it from Jundab ibn Sufyan al-Bajali, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was struck in his finger by a stone, so it bled, and he said: [*Are you anything but a finger that bled? And in the way of Allah you have suffered what you have suffered.*] Then he stayed a night or two nights or three without standing in prayer at night. Umm Jamil, the wife of Abu Lahab, said to him: "I do not think your devil has left you except that he has forsaken you. I have not seen him come near you for two nights or three." So the surah was revealed: ﴿By the morning brightness...﴾

He also related from Abu Imran al-Jawni, who said: Jibril was slow to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) until it distressed him. Then Jibril came while he had placed his forehead on the Ka'bah, supplicating, and a mark was made between his shoulders, and this was revealed to him: ﴿Your Lord has neither forsaken you nor come to hate you.﴾

Khawlah, who used to serve the Prophet (ﷺ), said: A puppy entered the house and went under the bed and died. The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) remained for days without revelation coming to him. He said: [*O Khawlah, what has happened in my house? Why does Jibril not come to me?*] Khawlah said: I said: "If I were to prepare the house and sweep it." So I struck with the broom under the bed, and there was a dead puppy. I took it and threw it behind the wall. Then the Prophet of Allah came, his jaws trembling, and when revelation came down upon him he was seized by trembling. He said: [*O Khawlah, wrap me up.*] So Allah revealed this surah. When Jibril came down, the Prophet (ﷺ) asked him about the delay, and he said: [*Do you not know that we do not enter a house in which there is a dog or a picture?*]

It has also been said: When the Jews asked him about the Spirit, Dhu'l-Qarnayn and the People of the Cave, he said: [*I will inform you tomorrow*], and he did not say "if Allah wills." *Wadda'aka* with the doubled letter (*tashdid*) is the reading of the majority (*al-ammah*), from *at-tawdi'*, which is like the farewell of one who departs. It is reported from Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr that they read *wada'aka* with a single letter (*takhfif*), meaning "left you." One poet said:

*"And there we left the family of Amr and Amir,*
*as prey for the tips of the dark spears."* [[*Al-muthaqqafah* and *al-mithqaf* mean the spear.]]

Its use is rare. One says: *huwa yada'u kadha*, meaning he leaves such-and-such. Al-Mubarrad Muhammad ibn Yazid said: They hardly ever say *wada'a* or *wadhara*, because the waw is weak when it comes first, and they dispensed with it by using *taraka*.

God Most High says: ﴿And has not hated you﴾, meaning your Lord has not hated you since He loved you. He omitted the *kaf* [the final "-ka" pronoun], because it is the end of a verse (*ra's ayah*). *Al-qila* means hatred. If you open the *qaf*, you lengthen it: one says *qalahu yaqlihi qilan wa qala'an*, just as one says *qara'tu ad-dayfa uqriuhu qira wa qira'*. *Yaqlah* [with the vowel on the *qaf* as above] is the dialect of Tayy. Tha'lab recited:

*"Days [[So in al-Lisan. In the originals: "Oh my Lord." After it, as in al-Lisan: "Even if she were to choose, her eyes would be pleasing (to the hearts)."]] of Umm al-Ghamr, we do not hate her."*

That is, we do not hate her. *Naqla* means we hate. Kuthayyir Izzah said:

*"Treat us badly or treat us well; she is not blamed by us,*
*nor is she hated by us if she turns away."*

Imru' al-Qays said:

*"And I am not one who hates the friendships, nor one who abandons."* [[The first half of the line: "I turned away from them out of fear of destruction." [...]]]

The interpretation of the verse is: Your Lord has neither forsaken you nor hated you. He omitted the *kaf* because it is the end of a verse, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿and the men who remember Allah much and the women who remember﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:35], meaning *wal-dhakirat Allah*, "and the women who remember Allah."

Al-Tha'labi also mentioned it from Jundab ibn Sufyan al-Bajali, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was struck in his finger by a stone, so it bled, and he said: [*Are you anything but a finger that bled? And in the way of Allah you have suffered what you have suffered.*] Then he stayed a night or two nights or three without standing in prayer at night. Umm Jamil, the wife of Abu Lahab, said to him: "I do not think your devil has left you except that he has forsaken you. I have not seen him come near you for two nights or three." So the surah was revealed: ﴿By the morning brightness...﴾

He also related from Abu Imran al-Jawni, who said: Jibril was slow to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) until it distressed him. Then Jibril came while he had placed his forehead on the Ka'bah, supplicating, and a mark was made between his shoulders, and this was revealed to him: ﴿Your Lord has neither forsaken you nor come to hate you.﴾

Khawlah, who used to serve the Prophet (ﷺ), said: A puppy entered the house and went under the bed and died. The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) remained for days without revelation coming to him. He said: [*O Khawlah, what has happened in my house? Why does Jibril not come to me?*] Khawlah said: I said: "If I were to prepare the house and sweep it." So I struck with the broom under the bed, and there was a dead puppy. I took it and threw it behind the wall. Then the Prophet of Allah came, his jaws trembling, and when revelation came down upon him he was seized by trembling. He said: [*O Khawlah, wrap me up.*] So Allah revealed this surah. When Jibril came down, the Prophet (ﷺ) asked him about the delay, and he said: [*Do you not know that we do not enter a house in which there is a dog or a picture?*]

It has also been said: When the Jews asked him about the Spirit, Dhu'l-Qarnayn and the People of the Cave, he said: [*I will inform you tomorrow*], and he did not say "if Allah wills." So revelation was withheld from him until Jibril came down to him with the words: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow," unless [adding], "If Allah wills"﴾ [al-Kahf 18:23–24]. So he informed him of what he had been asked about. In connection with this incident the words ﴿Your Lord has neither forsaken you nor come to hate you﴾ were revealed.

It has also been said that the Muslims said: "O Messenger of Allah, why does revelation not come down to you?" He said: [*How would it come down to me when you do not clean your knuckles*, and in another narration *your finger-joints* [[*Al-rawajib* (singular *rajibah*) is the space between the joints of the fingers. *Al-baraji* (singular *barjamah*, with a dammah) are the joints on the backs of the fingers where dirt collects.]], *and you do not trim your nails and you do not take from your moustaches*.] Then Jibril came down with this surah, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: [*You came only after I had longed for you.*] Jibril said: [*I was more longing for you, but I am a commanded servant.*] Then it was revealed to him: ﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord﴾ [Maryam 19:64].

*Wadda'aka* with the doubled letter (*tashdid*) is the reading of the majority (*al-ammah*), from *at-tawdi'*, which is like the farewell of one who departs. It is reported from Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Zubayr that they read *wada'aka* with a single letter (*takhfif*), meaning "left you." One poet said:

*"And there we left the family of Amr and Amir,*
*as prey for the tips of the dark spears."* [[*Al-muthaqqafah* and *al-mithqaf* mean the spear.]]

Its use is rare. One says: *huwa yada'u kadha*, meaning he leaves such-and-such. Al-Mubarrad Muhammad ibn Yazid said: They hardly ever say *wada'a* or *wadhara*, because the waw is weak when it comes first, and they dispensed with it by using *taraka*.

God Most High says: ﴿And has not hated you﴾, meaning your Lord has not hated you since He loved you. He omitted the *kaf* [the final "-ka" pronoun], because it is the end of a verse (*ra's ayah*). *Al-qila* means hatred. If you open the *qaf*, you lengthen it: one says *qalahu yaqlihi qilan wa qala'an*, just as one says *qara'tu ad-dayfa uqriuhu qira wa qira'*. *Yaqlah* [with the vowel on the *qaf* as above] is the dialect of Tayy. Tha'lab recited:

*"Days [[So in al-Lisan. In the originals: "Oh my Lord." After it, as in al-Lisan: "Even if she were to choose, her eyes would be pleasing (to the hearts)."]] of Umm al-Ghamr, we do not hate her."*

That is, we do not hate her. *Naqla* means we hate. Kuthayyir Izzah said:

*"Treat us badly or treat us well; she is not blamed by us,*
*nor is she hated by us if she turns away."*

Imru' al-Qays said:

*"And I am not one who hates the friendships, nor one who abandons."* [[The first half of the line: "I turned away from them out of fear of destruction." [...]]]

The interpretation of the verse is: Your Lord has neither forsaken you nor hated you. He omitted the *kaf* because it is the end of a verse, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿and the men who remember Allah much and the women who remember﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:35], meaning *wal-dhakirat Allah*, "and the women who remember Allah."

Salamah narrated from Ibn Ishaq, who said: "And the Hereafter is better for you than the first." That is, what I have in store for you when you return to Me, O Muhammad, is better for you than the honour I have hastened for you in this world.

Ibn 'Abbas said: The Prophet ﷺ was shown what Allah would open to his community after him, and he was delighted by it. Then Jibril descended with: "And the Hereafter is better for you than the first. And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied."

Ibn Ishaq said: [The better thing is] the victory in this world and the reward in the Hereafter. It was also said: [It refers to] the Basin (al-Hawd) and intercession (al-Shafa'ah).

From Ibn 'Abbas: [It is] a thousand palaces of white pearl, whose dust is musk. Al-Awza'i traced it back (rafa'ahu), saying: Isma'il ibn 'Ubayd Allah narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas, from his father, who said: The Prophet ﷺ was shown what would be opened to his community, and he was delighted by it. So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "By the morning brightness... to His words, Exalted is He: And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied." So Allah, may His praise be exalted, gave him a thousand palaces in Paradise, whose dust is musk, and in each palace is whatever spouses and servants befit him.

Also from him [Ibn 'Abbas] he said: Muhammad was content that none of the people of his household would enter the Fire.

Al-Suddi said [something similar]. It was also said: It is intercession for all the believers.

From 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah will grant me intercession for my community until Allah, glorified is He, says to me: 'Are you content, O Muhammad?' And I will say: 'O Lord, I am content.'"

In Sahih Muslim, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, that the Prophet ﷺ recited the words of Allah, the Exalted, concerning Ibrahim: "Whoever follows me, then he is of me; and whoever disobeys me, then indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful" [Ibrahim: 36], and the words of 'Isa: "If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants; and if You forgive them, indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise" [al-Ma'idah: 118]. Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 93, verse 6:

He (glory be to Him) enumerated His favours upon His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), saying: ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?﴾ ﴿Did He not find you an orphan, without a father? Your father died.﴾ So "fa-awa" means He made for you a refuge to which you could turn, through your uncle Abu Talib, and so he took care of you.

It was said to Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq: Why was the Prophet (ﷺ) left an orphan from both his parents? He said: So that no created being would have a claim upon him.

And on the authority of Mujahid: it comes from the saying of the Arabs, "a unique pearl (durrah yatimah)," when it has no equal. So the meaning of the verse is: Did He not find you unique in your nobility, with no equal, and so Allah sheltered you with companions who would guard you and surround you.

﴿And He found you lost, and guided [you]﴾ (93:7). That is, unaware of what was intended for you concerning the matter of prophethood. "Guided" means He set you on the right way. Here "lost" (ḍāll) carries the sense of heedlessness, as in His saying, exalted is His praise: ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾ (20:52), meaning He does not become heedless. And concerning His Prophet He said: ﴿And indeed you were before it among the heedless﴾ (12:3).

Some said: "lost" means you did not know the Qur'an and the sharia, so God guided you to the Qur'an and the laws of Islam. This is related from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Shahr ibn Ḥawshab and others. It is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor faith﴾ (42:52), as we explained in the surah "al-Shūrā."

Some said: ﴿And He found you lost﴾ means among a people who were lost, so God guided them through you. This is the view of al-Kalbī and al-Farrā'. Al-Suddī related something similar, meaning: He found your people in error, so He guided you to guide them.

It was also said: He found you lost concerning the Hijra, so He guided you to it.

It was also said: "lost" means forgetful of the matter of the exception (istithnā') when you were asked about the People of the Cave, Dhū al-Qarnayn and the Spirit, so He reminded you, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That one of them should err, and the other remind her﴾ (2:282).

It was also said: He found you seeking the qibla, so He guided you to it. Its proof is: ﴿We have seen the turning of your face toward the sky﴾ (2:144), and the verse continues.

"Lost" may also mean "seeking," since the one who is lost is seeking. And it was said: He found you bewildered about explaining what was revealed to you, so He guided you to it. Then "lost" means "bewildered," since the one who is lost is bewildered.

It was also said: He found you lost among your people, so He guided you to them. Then "lost" means "perishing."

It was also said: He found you loving guidance, so He guided you to it. Then "lost" means "love." From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "By God, you are indeed in your old error"﴾ (12:95), meaning in your love.

The poet said:

"This error has whitened my middle head
and both my cheeks, though I was not one who had been sure."

"Wonder at ʿAzza, in her choosing to cut me off
after the error, though her rope has worn out."

Some said: "lost" in the ravines of Mecca, so He guided him and returned him to his grandfather ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. Ibn ʿAbbās said: The Prophet (ﷺ), while still young, strayed in the ravines of Mecca, and Abū Jahl saw him wandering away from his flocks and returned him to his grandfather ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. God showed favor to him in that, when He returned him to his grandfather through the hands of his enemy.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: The Prophet (ﷺ) went out with his uncle Abū Ṭālib on a journey. On a dark night Iblīs took hold of the she-camel's halter and turned her from the road. Then Jibrīl (peace be upon him) came, blew upon Iblīs a blast which sent him down to the land of India, and returned him to the caravan. God showed favor to him in that.

Kaʿb said: When Ḥalīma had fulfilled her duty of nursing, she brought the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to return him to ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. At the gate of Mecca she heard: "Congratulations to you, O valley of Mecca! Today light, religion, splendor and beauty are returned to you." She said: "I set him down to arrange my garments, and I heard a mighty crash. I turned and did not see him. I said: 'O people, where is the boy?' They said: 'We have seen nothing.' I cried: 'Wā Muḥammadāh!' Then there was an aged old man leaning on his staff, who said: 'Go to the greatest idol. If he wishes to return him to you, he will.' The old man circled the idol and kissed its head, saying: 'O Lord, Your favor upon Quraysh has never ceased. This Saʿdiyya claims her son has gone astray, so return him, if You wish.' Then Hubal fell on its face, and the idols toppled, and they said: 'Away from us, old man! Why were we not, instead, at the hands of Muḥammad?' The old man threw down his staff, trembled and said: 'Your son has a Lord who will not neglect him, so seek him calmly.'" Then Quraysh gathered to ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, and they searched for him throughout Mecca but did not find him. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib circled the Kaʿba seven times and humbly asked God to return him, saying:

"O Lord, return my son Muḥammad,
return him, my Lord, and make a hand with me.
O Lord, if Muḥammad is not found,
the whole of my people's unity is scattered."

Then they heard a caller calling from the sky: "O people, do not clamor. Muḥammad has a Lord who will not forsake him or neglect him. Muḥammad is in the valley of Tihāma, by the tree of the samur." So ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib set out, together with Waraqa ibn Nawfal, and there was the Prophet (ﷺ) standing under a tree, playing with its branches and leaves.

It was also said: ﴿And He found you lost﴾ on the night of the Ascension, when Jibrīl left you while you did not know the way, so He guided you to the lote-tree of the Throne (sidrat al-muntahā) (cf. 53:14).

Abū Bakr al-Warrāq and others said: ﴿And He found you lost﴾: you loved Abū Ṭālib, so He guided you to love of your Lord.

Bassām ibn ʿAbd Allāh said: ﴿And He found you lost﴾ within yourself, not knowing who you were, so He made you know yourself and your state.

Al-Junaydī said: He found you bewildered about explaining the Book, so He taught you the explanation. Its proof is: ﴿That you may make clear to mankind what has been sent down to them﴾ (16:44), and the verse continues, ﴿that you may make clear to them that about which they differ﴾ (16:64).

Some of the speakers (mutakallimūn) said: When the Arabs find a solitary tree in a barren wilderness with no other trees near it, they call it "lost" (ḍālla), and people are guided by it to the road. So God, exalted is He, said to His Prophet Muḥammad (ﷺ): ﴿And He found you lost﴾, that is, there was no one on your religion, and you were alone with no one with you, so I guided through you the creation to Me.

I say: All these opinions are good. Some of them are figurative and some literal. The last opinion pleases me most, because it encompasses the figurative opinions.

Some said: He was upon the general condition of his people, showing no opposition to them outwardly. As for polytheism, it is not to be supposed of him. Rather, he followed the customs of his people outwardly for forty years.

Al-Kalbī and al-Suddī said: This is to be taken literally, that is, He found you a disbeliever while your people were disbelievers, so He guided you.[[Such opinions cannot be attributed to the master of creation, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, nor to any of the prophets, because according to the sound view infallibility (ʿiṣma) is established for them before and after prophethood, from major and minor sins.]]

This opinion and the refutation of it have already been mentioned in the surah "al-Shūrā."[[See vol. 16, p. 55 and following.]] It was also said: He found you immersed among the people of polytheism, so He distinguished you from them. It is said: "The water got lost in the milk" (ḍalla al-māʾ fī al-laban), and from this is His saying: ﴿When we are lost in the earth﴾ (32:10), meaning when we are mixed with the dust at burial, until it is as if we are not distinguished from its whole.

In the reading of al-Ḥasan: ﴿And He found you the lost one, and He guided﴾, meaning the lost one found guidance through you. This is a reading that serves as an interpretation.

It was also said: He found you lost, without your people being guided to you or recognizing your rank, so He guided the Muslims to you, until they believed in you.

And He found you in need and enriched you. [Al-Qurtubi:] That is, poor, having no wealth. "And enriched you" means He enriched you through Khadijah, may Allah be pleased with her. It is said: "al-rajul ya'il ay'ilah" (the man became poor) when he became destitute. Uhayhah ibn al-Julah said:

"The poor man does not know when his riches will come, nor does the rich man know when he will become needy."

That is, he will become poor. Muqatil said: He satisfied you with the provision He gave you. Al-Kalbi said: He made you content with provision. Ibn 'Ata' said: He found you poor in soul, and so He enriched your heart. Al-Akhfash said: He found you with dependents, the evidence for which is "and enriched you." From this is the verse of Jarir:

"Allah sent down in the Book an obligation for the wayfarer and for the needy dependent."

It is also said: He found you lacking in proofs and evidences, and so He enriched you with them. It is also said: He enriched you with the conquests He opened for you and the wealth of the disbelievers that He granted you. Al-Qushayri said: There is room for scrutiny here, because the surah is Meccan, and jihad was only made obligatory in Medina. The common recitation is "'a'ilan." Ibn al-Sumayqa read "'ayyilan" with shaddah, like "tayyib" and "hayyin."

**Issue 1:** Concerning Allah's words, ﴿So as for the orphan, do not oppress him﴾. That is, do not domineer over him with injustice. Give him his right, and remember your own orphanhood. This is the view of al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash, a grammarian). It was also said that the two words are dialects with the same meaning. From Mujahid, "do not oppress" means "do not belittle." Al-Nakha'i and al-Ash'hab al-'Uqayli read *takhhar* (تَكْهَرْ) with a *kaf*, and it is written the same way in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud. On this reading, the verse may be a prohibition against oppressing him, by wronging him and taking his property. He is singled out because he has no helper other than Allah, the Exalted, so the command concerning him is stressed by making the punishment for his oppressor severe. The Arabs interchange *kaf* and *qaf*. Al-Nahhas (a grammarian and exegete) said: This is an error. It is only said *kahharahu* when one is harsh with someone and treats him roughly.

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Mu'awiya ibn al-Hakam al-Sulami, when he spoke during the prayer by returning a greeting, he said: "May my father and mother be sacrificed for him! I have never seen a teacher before him or after him better in teaching than him, meaning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). By Allah, he neither scolded me, nor struck me, nor insulted me..." (the hadith continues).

It was also said: *al-qahr* is overpowering, and *al-kahr* is rebuking.

**Issue 2:** The verse indicates gentleness toward the orphan, kindness to him, and benevolence toward him, to the extent that Qatadah said: "Be to the orphan like a merciful father."

It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah that a man complained to the Prophet (ﷺ) of the hardness of his heart, and he said: "If you wish for your heart to soften, stroke the head of the orphan and feed the needy."

In the Sahih, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I and the one who sponsors an orphan, whether his own or another's, are like these two," and he pointed with the index and middle fingers.

From the hadith of Ibn Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the orphan weeps, the Throne of the Merciful shakes because of his weeping. Then Allah, the Exalted, says to His angels: 'O My angels, who has made this orphan weep, whose father I have hidden in the dust?' The angels say: 'Our Lord, You know best.' Then Allah, the Exalted, says to His angels: 'O My angels, bear witness that whoever silences him and pleases him, I will please him on the Day of Resurrection.'" So Ibn Umar, whenever he saw an orphan, would stroke his head and give him something.

From Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever takes in an orphan and supports him in his maintenance and relieves him of his burden, he will have a shield from the Fire on the Day of Resurrection. And whoever strokes the head of an orphan, he will have a good deed for every hair." Aktham ibn Sayfi said: "The humiliated are four: the tale-bearer, the liar, the one in debt, and the orphan."

**Issue 3:** Allah's words, ﴿And as for the one who asks, do not drive him away﴾. That is, do not rebuke him. This is a prohibition against harsh speech. Rather, turn him away with a little giving or with a gracious refusal, and mention your own poverty. This was said by Qatadah and others.

It is narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Let none of you withhold from the beggar, and let him give to him when he asks, even if he sees two bracelets of gold in his hand." Ibrahim ibn Adham said: "What excellent people the beggars are! They carry our provision to the Hereafter." Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: "The beggar is the mail-courier of the Hereafter. He comes to the door of one of you and says: 'Will you send anything to your families?'"

It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Turn the beggar away with a little giving or a gracious refusal, for there will come to you one who is neither of mankind nor of the jinn, who looks at how you act with what Allah has entrusted to you."

As for its being established as a Sunnah by single-transmitter reports (*naql al-ahad*), Ibn Kathir considered it recommended (*mustahabb*), not obligatory, and he did not declare those who omit it to be in error.

Al-Hakim Abu Abdullah Muhammad ibn Abdullah al-Hafiz mentioned in his book *al-Mustadrak* on (the authorities of) al-Bukhari and Muslim: Abu Yahya Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Yazid, the reciter and imam in Makkah, in the Masjid al-Haram, told us, saying: Abu Abdullah Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Zayd al-Sa'igh told us, saying: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah told us: I heard Ikrimah ibn Sulayman say: "I recited to Isma'il ibn Abdullah ibn Qustantin, and when I reached *Surat al-Duha*, he said to me: 'Say *takbir* at the end of every surah until you finish, for I recited to Abdullah ibn Kathir, and when I reached *Surat al-Duha*, he said: Say *takbir* until you finish.'" Abdullah ibn Kathir informed him that he recited to Mujahid, and Mujahid informed him that Ibn Abbas ordered him to do this, and Ibn Abbas informed him that Ubayy ibn Ka'b ordered him to do this, and Ubayy ibn Ka'b informed him that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered him to do this. This is a sound hadith, though al-Bukhari and Muslim did not record it.
